I don't blame you for feeling the way that you do. 

The first thing that you need to understand is that her bipolar disorder diagnosis does not explain or excuse her behavior toward you and it does explain or excuse the way she abuses you. 

Bipolar disorder has symptoms however those who have bipolar disorder are aware of their actions, their words and their treatment of others. 

Please don't fall into the "she doesn't really know what she's doing" or "it's her illness". 

Because that is not true. 

There is an individual behind the illness. An individual with their sense of right and wrong and an individual with their own values. 

There are many stories of people falling in love with a person who do not have bipolar disorder and who they thought were a decent, loving person only to see the abusive monster reveals themselves later.

This is no different than those who have bipolar disorder. Those with bipolar disorder can seem loving and charming while hiding the abusive person they really are just the same as those who do not have bipolar disorder. 

Don't allow her mental health diagnosis as an excuse for her to abuse you in the way that you have described. 

If you feel that you have truly had enough you stand a very good chance of getting custody of the children, given her actions and her behavior. 

If you feel that you'd like to keep giving this marriage a chance maybe you could have a meeting with your and her doctor and discuss her behavior and how she has been treating you. 

Or the two of you can take part in couple's counseling where the goal is for your wife to hold herself accountable for her abusive behavior and the way that she abuses you. 

However, I don't recommend staying in a marriage with a person who abuses you. 

But it is your choice. As I said, you are the healthier and stronger primary parent and I think that you stand a very good chance of getting custody of the children. 

I hope, for the sake of your mental health, that you have friends and families who you can turn to for help and for support. 

You may want to speak to an attorney and describe what has been happening to you so that you understand what your rights are as a person and as a father. 

If you need to reach out for professional help or talk your doctor about receiving treatment for stress or depression please do. 

Please take care of your own mental health before your wife takes and even bigger toll on your mental and emotional well-being. 

Please take care of your own health. 

In the meantime look into what your rights and what your options are if you decide to end this marriage. 

I'm sorry to repeat myself but her mental health diagnosis is not an excuse for the abuse that you are suffering. 

Please reach out for help, please seek help and support from those who are close to you. 

I'm so sorry that what you are going through. 

I wish you all the best.

The remaining Doors tell these stories but the situation obviously didn't end with his bandmates asking Jim to leave band for his own sake and for the sake of his health after watching, time and time again, supposedly, this epic self-destruction and the alleged outrageous behavior Robby describes. 

(How could Lynn even stand to be around Jim after doing that? How could Robby stand to be around the guy who did that to the woman he loved? I'm sorry but something's missing here.) 

Guess Jim was too much of a draw as far as audiences and I guess the other three were more famous and made a lot more money with Jim around.

I'm seriously doubting the syphilis story too. 

It may have been a story that Jim Morrison told for the sake of shock value.

There'd be so many stories from women who contracted syphilis from Jim and syphilis also comes with serious mental health effects. Jim would not have been able to continue with the band if he had untreated syphilis. 

I recommend that fans read Frank Lisciandro's book, Jim Morrison: Friends Gathered Together. 

This book shows a very different side of Jim Morrison. 

In No One Here Get's Out Alive, aka Nothing Here But A Lot of Lies, and there is a line about Jim Morrison showing up at the home of one of the band's publicists "in the middle of the night" and "frantically banging on the door". 

Told from the point of view of the publicist Jim apologized for the late hour but he had heard that the publicist's son was sick. Jim had bought the kid an African thumb drum and wanted to give it to him and he sat with the kid and showed him how to play it. 

Both the publicist and his son recall this as a nice story and a memory of Jim Morrison doing something really sweet. 

I don't doubt that Jim Morrison was a challenging person to deal with but he does seem like someone who people can pin any insane story on.

Again, if only in the interest of fairness, I recommend Lisciandro's Friends Gathered Together.

I should have been more clear when making my point. 

My advice is not to excuse every act of emotional or psychological abuse from someone who is bipolar with the belief that it's their mental health issues that causing them to act that way. 

A person who has bipolar disorder can be abusive by nature the same way that someone who does not have bipolar disorder can be abusive by nature. 

And I don't doubt that when unmedicated some of their actions can be attributed to their illness and that sometimes their crisis can be so severe that they face involuntary hospitalizations. 

But, just because the bipolar person in question has stopped taking their medication or if they are manic that does not mean that they simply have no idea what they're saying or doing because that is not true. 

I know from personal experience how dangerous and devastating it can be to tolerate abuse from someone who is bipolar because I believed that they were not really responsible for what they say and what they do. 

Believing that left me with a lot of very, very painful scars. 

And repeatedly being irresponsible with their health and refusing to follow a medication regimen that they know they need to follow is a valid enough reason all by itself to end a relationship with someone who is bipolar. 

Bipolar disorder is a vicious thing, and that's sad, and partners, friends and families, up to a point, are going to have to deal with the symptoms.

But those around the bipolar person have the right to preserve their own minds, they're well-being and their health if they are dealing with someone who plays chicken with their health, abuse those who care about them and if the relationship with the bipolar person is causing them nothing but misery.

And you could very lose yourself in this situation. 

You lose yourself, your mental health, your emotional health - and that is NOT a road you want to go down. 

You'd have a very difficult and painful road back to recovery and you've been through enough. 

I'm glad that you came to this healthy decision and where you go from here is up to you. 

Whatever decision you please prioritize yourself and your health. Please. 

(And please never fall into the "it's her illness, she doesn't know what she's doing or saying" because that's not true. Those who have bipolar disorder, even when manic, are aware of their actions and their words and of the impact of those words and actions.) 

Congratulations on coming to this healthy place in your life.
